revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Surveys and Statistics
revealWordProblem.text: Some sixth-grade students want to get more food choices in the cafeteria. They will conduct a survey of students who buy lunch in the cafeteria. What questions should they include in their survey? Explain your choices.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: A good survey question must be a statistical question — one that anticipates variability, since different students will give different answers. Two strong choices: 'On a scale of 1 to 5, how satisfied are you with the current cafeteria food choices?' and 'Which new lunch item would you most like to see added: pizza, tacos, a salad bar, or stir-fry?' Both work because the answers will differ from student to student and can be tallied — for example, if 45 out of 80 students surveyed pick tacos, that's 45 ÷ 80 = 0.5625 = 56.25% of respondents, showing tacos as the clear favorite to petition for. A question like 'How many days a week does the cafeteria serve lunch?' would NOT belong on the survey, because it has one fixed answer for every student and doesn't anticipate variability.

turnAndTalk.kernel: A statistical question expects answers that vary across many cases.

stems.en: The other question is not statistical because it has only ___ answer.
stems.es: La otra pregunta no es estadística porque tiene solo ___ respuesta.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students identify "How tall is each player?" as statistical because heights vary, while "How tall is our point guard?" has one fixed answer.
turnAndTalk.extend: Take a non-statistical question and reword it so it becomes statistical. Explain exactly what you changed to create variability.
extendStems: I changed it to "___" so the answers will ___.

turnAndTalk.question: While sorting the questions, what clue tells you instantly that a question will need DATA from many players to answer?

turnAndTalk.listenFor: A strong answer notes words like "each" or "per player" signal variability, so you must collect data from many cases rather than look up one fact.
turnAndTalk.extend: Is it possible for a question with a numerical answer to still be NOT statistical? Justify with an example from the basketball league.
extendStems: Yes, a question like "___" has numbers but is not statistical because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: The newspaper editor prefers "How many goals did each player score?" over "How many goals did the team score total?" Which gives more interesting data for a story?

stems.en: The editor's question is better because it shows ___ among players.

stems.en: The total only gives ___ number, so it hides ___.
stems.es: El total solo da ___ número, así que oculta ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students explain the per-player question is statistical and shows variability (who scored most/least), while the total is one fixed number that hides individual differences.
turnAndTalk.extend: Critique the reporter's plan: when might a single total actually be the RIGHT thing to report instead of per-player data? Defend your view.
extendStems: A total would be better when the reader wants to know ___.

turnAndTalk.question: Think of one statistical question you could ask about students in this room. What variability do you expect in the answers?
turnAndTalk.kernel: A good statistical question is answered by collecting varied data, not one fact.
turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students pose a question whose answers vary across classmates and name the variability they expect (e.g., different bedtimes, different shoe sizes).
turnAndTalk.extend: Generalize: what is the one test you can always run on any question to decide if it is statistical? State your rule in one sentence.
extendStems: My rule is: a question is statistical if ___.
I can test any question by asking whether the answers will ___.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice on Statistical Questions and Data, what strategy did you use when a problem felt tricky?
turnAndTalk.kernel: If you expect the answers to vary, it is a statistical question.

vocabulary.definition: A statistical question expects varied answers that can be collected as data.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una pregunta estadística espera respuestas variadas que se pueden recopilar como datos.
vocabulary.visual: How many minutes do students in our class read each night?

vocabulary.definition: A question where the answers will be different for different people.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una pregunta cuyas respuestas serán distintas para distintas personas.
vocabulary.visual: “How tall are the players on the team?” → answers vary: 60 in, 63 in, 58 in, 65 in
vocabulary.cloze: A question that expects a variety of answers and is answered by collecting data is a ___.

examples.text: How tall are the students in my class?
examples.why: The answers vary, so data must be collected.
It has one fixed answer, so it is not statistical.

vocabulary.definition: A question that has just one fixed answer that is the same no matter who you ask, so there is no data to collect.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una pregunta que tiene una sola respuesta fija, igual sin importar a quién le preguntes, por lo que no hay datos que recolectar.
vocabulary.visual: “How tall am I?” → one answer: 60 in. Everyone who measures gets the same number.
vocabulary.cloze: A question that has one fixed answer and does not need data collection is a ___.

examples.text: How many days are in a week?
examples.why: The answer is always 7 — it never varies, so there is no data to collect.

examples.text: How tall are the students in my class?
examples.why: Different students have different heights, so the answers vary — that makes it statistical.

vocabulary.definition: Facts and numbers you collect, like answers to a survey.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Datos y números que recoges, como respuestas a una encuesta.
vocabulary.visual: Player heights: 60 in, 63 in, 58 in, 65 in — four different measurements
vocabulary.cloze: Facts or numbers collected to answer a question are ___.

vocabulary.definition: How spread out the numbers are.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Qué tan separados están los números.
vocabulary.visual: Scores 10, 12, 11 are close together (low variability); scores 2, 15, 30 are far apart (high variability)
vocabulary.cloze: How much the values in a data set differ from one another is the ___.

vocabulary.definition: Collecting facts by asking people questions.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Recoger datos haciendo preguntas a las personas.
vocabulary.visual: Asking 50 students 'What is your favorite sport?' and recording the answers
vocabulary.cloze: A way to collect data by asking many people the same question is a ___.

vocabulary.definition: How the data looks: where it sits and how spread out it is.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Cómo se ven los datos: dónde están y qué tan separados están.
vocabulary.visual: If most scores cluster in the middle with fewer at the edges, the distribution is symmetric
vocabulary.cloze: The way data values are spread out across a range is the ___.

Some questions will give you interesting data with variety, while others have just one fixed answer. Your job: figure out which questions are worth investigating with data.

conceptIntro.heading: What makes a question a statistical question?
conceptIntro.intro: A statistical question is one you answer by collecting data, and the answers are different for different people or cases. A non-statistical question has just one fixed answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: If you expect the answers to vary, it is a statistical question.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: Question 1: "How many points did our top player score last night?" There is one player and one game, so there is one fixed answer, like 18 points.
One answer, no variety, so this is NOT a statistical question.
Question 2: "How many points does each player score per game?" The answers vary: 8, 12, 12, 15, 18, 20, 22.
Because the answers are different for different players, I must collect data. This IS a statistical question.

weDo.title: Let's try together
lines: New question: "How many pets does each student in our class have?" Will every student give the same answer, or different answers?
Some students have 0 pets and others have 2 or 3, so the answers vary. Is this statistical or not statistical?
Now a different question: "How many days are in one week?" Does this have one fixed answer or many?

discourse.prompt: What pattern do you notice about statistical questions compared to non-statistical questions?
discourse.sentenceFrame: Statistical questions expect ___ in the answers because ___. Non-statistical questions have only ___ answer because ___.

optional.instructions: Drag each scouting question into the right bin. A statistical question expects answers that VARY from player to player; a non-statistical question has one fixed answer.

items.text: How many push-ups can each player on the team do in one minute?
items.textEs: ¿Cuántas lagartijas puede hacer cada jugador del equipo en un minuto?

items.text: How many points does each starter average per game?
items.textEs: ¿Cuántos puntos promedia cada titular por juego?

items.text: How many seconds does each player take to sprint the court?
items.textEs: ¿Cuántos segundos tarda cada jugador en cruzar la cancha?

items.text: How many free throws did each teammate make in practice?
items.textEs: ¿Cuántos tiros libres anotó cada compañero en la práctica?

items.text: How many players are allowed on the court at once?
items.textEs: ¿Cuántos jugadores se permiten en la cancha a la vez?

items.text: What is the diameter of an official basketball hoop?
items.textEs: ¿Cuál es el diámetro de un aro oficial de baloncesto?

items.text: How many quarters are played in one game?
items.textEs: ¿Cuántos cuartos se juegan en un partido?

optional.explanation: The four statistical cards all measure something for each player — push-ups, points averaged, sprint seconds, free throws made — so the answers form a set of different values. The other three ask about rules or equipment: players allowed on the court, hoop diameter, and quarters per game each have one fixed answer.
optional.explanationEs: Las cuatro tarjetas estadísticas miden algo de cada jugador —lagartijas, promedio de puntos, segundos de velocidad, tiros libres encestados—, así que las respuestas forman un conjunto de valores distintos. Las otras tres preguntan por reglas o equipo: los jugadores permitidos en la cancha, el diámetro del aro y los cuartos por partido tienen cada uno una sola respuesta fija.
hints: A statistical question expects answers that differ from player to player; a non-statistical one has a single fixed answer.
Scan each card for phrases like 'each player' or 'each teammate', and notice which cards ask about a rule or a piece of equipment instead.
Take the first card — push-ups in one minute for each player: would two teammates give the same number? Answer that before you drop it in a bin.
hintsEs: Una pregunta estadística espera respuestas que cambien de un jugador a otro; una no estadística tiene una sola respuesta fija.
Busca en cada tarjeta frases como 'cada jugador' o 'cada compañero', y fíjate en cuáles preguntan por una regla o por el equipo.
Toma la primera tarjeta: las lagartijas en un minuto de cada jugador. ¿Dos compañeros darían el mismo número? Responde eso antes de colocarla en un grupo.
optional.instructionsEs: Arrastra cada pregunta de exploración al grupo correcto. Una pregunta estadística espera respuestas que VARÍAN de un jugador a otro; una pregunta no estadística tiene una sola respuesta fija.

optional.stem: The team analyst writes four questions for the scouting report. Which one is a statistical question?
choices: How many rebounds does each player grab per game?
How many points is a single free throw worth?
What is the height of the basketball rim?
How many timeouts does each team get per half?
optional.explanation: "How many rebounds does each player grab per game?" anticipates variability — different players grab different numbers of rebounds, so you must collect data. The other three each have one fixed answer.
choiceFeedback: Numbers alone don't make it statistical—does this have variation across cases, or one fixed answer?
This measures one thing—would different answers come from different cases?
This follows a fixed rule for all teams—would you get different answers?
optional.stemEs: El analista del equipo escribe cuatro preguntas para el informe de exploración. ¿Cuál es una pregunta estadística?
optional.explanationEs: «¿Cuántos rebotes atrapa cada jugador por partido?» anticipa variabilidad: distintos jugadores atrapan distintos números de rebotes, así que hay que recolectar datos. Las otras tres tienen una sola respuesta fija.
hints: A statistical question expects the answers to vary; a non-statistical question has one fixed answer.
Read each choice and decide whether it would give you one answer or many different answers.
Check the rule-based choices first: things set by the rules of the game cannot vary, so rule those out and look at what is left.
hintsEs: Una pregunta estadística espera que las respuestas varíen; una pregunta no estadística tiene una sola respuesta fija.
Lee cada opción y decide si te daría una sola respuesta o muchas respuestas distintas.
Revisa primero las opciones basadas en reglas: lo que fijan las reglas del juego no puede variar, así que descarta esas y mira lo que queda.
choicesEs: ¿Cuántos rebotes atrapa cada jugador por partido?
¿Cuántos puntos vale un tiro libre?
¿Cuál es la altura del aro de baloncesto?
¿Cuántos tiempos fuera tiene cada equipo por mitad?

optional.stem: Why does the question "How many minutes did each athlete warm up before the game?" count as a statistical question?
choices: Because the warm-up times will vary from one athlete to another
Because the answer is measured in minutes
Because every athlete warmed up for exactly the same time
Because it is about a sports team
optional.explanation: A statistical question anticipates variability. Different athletes warm up for different amounts of time, so the data you collect will vary.
choiceFeedback: Measurements in minutes are used in both types—what about this makes it statistical?
If every athlete warmed the same amount, would the question need data?
Being about sports doesn't make it statistical—look for variability.
optional.stemEs: ¿Por qué la pregunta «¿Cuántos minutos calentó cada atleta antes del partido?» cuenta como una pregunta estadística?
optional.explanationEs: Una pregunta estadística anticipa variabilidad. Distintos atletas calientan durante tiempos distintos, así que los datos que recolectes van a variar.
hints: The test for a statistical question is variability, not the topic or the units used.
Imagine collecting an answer from every athlete. Would the list be all the same number, or a mix of numbers?
Picture two athletes' warm-up times side by side. If those two numbers could be different, use that to decide what makes the question statistical.
hintsEs: La prueba para una pregunta estadística es la variabilidad, no el tema ni las unidades que se usan.
Imagina que recoges una respuesta de cada atleta. ¿Sería la lista siempre el mismo número o una mezcla de números?
Imagina los tiempos de calentamiento de dos atletas uno al lado del otro. Si esos dos números podrían ser distintos, usa eso para decidir qué hace estadística a la pregunta.
choicesEs: Porque los tiempos de calentamiento varían de un atleta a otro
Porque la respuesta se mide en minutos
Porque todos los atletas calentaron exactamente el mismo tiempo
Porque es sobre un equipo deportivo

optional.label: Match each weak (non-statistical) scouting question to a stronger version that becomes statistical by adding variability.

pairs.term: How many players are on the roster?
pairs.match: How many minutes does each player on the roster play per game?
pairs.matchEs: ¿Cuántos minutos juega cada jugador de la plantilla por partido?

pairs.term: What time does the game start?
pairs.match: What time does each fan arrive at the arena?
pairs.matchEs: ¿A qué hora llega cada aficionado a la arena?

pairs.term: How long is the basketball court?
pairs.match: How far from the hoop does each player shoot most often?
pairs.matchEs: ¿Desde qué distancia del aro tira cada jugador con más frecuencia?

pairs.term: How many points did the team score in total?
pairs.match: How many points did each player score in the game?
pairs.termEs: ¿Cuántos puntos anotó el equipo en total?
pairs.matchEs: ¿Cuántos puntos anotó cada jugador en el partido?

optional.explanation: Each weak question has one fixed answer, and its stronger partner keeps the topic but measures every person or moment: roster size becomes minutes played by each player, the game's start time becomes each fan's arrival time, the court's length becomes each player's usual shooting distance, and the team total becomes points scored by each player.
optional.explanationEs: Cada pregunta débil tiene una sola respuesta fija, y su versión más fuerte mantiene el tema pero mide a cada persona o momento: el tamaño de la plantilla se convierte en los minutos que juega cada jugador, la hora de inicio del partido en la hora de llegada de cada aficionado, el largo de la cancha en la distancia desde la que suele tirar cada jugador, y el total del equipo en los puntos que anotó cada jugador.
hints: A weak question has a single fixed answer; its stronger partner asks about EACH person so the answers can vary.
For each weak card, look for the version that keeps the same topic but measures many people or many moments.
Start with 'How many players are on the roster?' — that is one count. Find the card that measures something for each player on that same roster.
hintsEs: Una pregunta débil tiene una sola respuesta fija; su pareja más fuerte pregunta por CADA persona para que las respuestas puedan variar.
Para cada tarjeta débil, busca la versión que mantiene el mismo tema pero mide a muchas personas o muchos momentos.
Empieza con '¿Cuántos jugadores hay en la plantilla?': eso es un solo conteo. Busca la tarjeta que mide algo de cada jugador de esa misma plantilla.
optional.labelEs: Une cada pregunta débil (no estadística) con una versión más fuerte que se vuelve estadística al agregar variabilidad.

optional.title: Level 2 Extension — A Misclassified Scouting Question

workedExample.label: Question
workedExample.work: How many goals did the league's top scorer net this season?
workedExample.workEs: ¿Cuántos goles anotó esta temporada el máximo goleador de la liga?

workedExample.label: Student decision
workedExample.work: This is NOT a statistical question.
workedExample.workEs: Esta NO es una pregunta estadística.

workedExample.label: Student reason
workedExample.work: It names only one player, so there can be no variability in the answers.
workedExample.workEs: Nombra a un solo jugador, así que no puede haber variabilidad en las respuestas.

optional.correctWork: The reason is wrong. "This season" covers many games, and the player scores a different number of goals in each game. Because the data varies from game to game, the question DOES anticipate variability — so it IS a statistical question.
hints: Ask whether the data would have different values across the many games in a season.
Variability can come from many games for one player, not just from many players.
optional.titleEs: Extensión de Nivel 2 — una pregunta de exploración mal clasificada
optional.explanation: The reasoning step assumes that naming one player rules out variability, but 'this season' spans many games and the goal count changes from game to game. Variability can come from many games for a single player, so the question is statistical.
optional.explanationEs: El paso del razonamiento supone que nombrar a un solo jugador descarta la variabilidad, pero 'esta temporada' abarca muchos partidos y la cantidad de goles cambia de un partido a otro. La variabilidad puede venir de muchos partidos de un solo jugador, así que la pregunta sí es estadística.
optional.correctWorkEs: La razón está mal. 'Esta temporada' abarca muchos partidos, y el jugador anota un número diferente de goles en cada uno. Como los datos varían de partido a partido, la pregunta SÍ anticipa variabilidad — así que SÍ es una pregunta estadística.

approaching.stem: Which of the following is a statistical question?
choices: How many points did each player score this season?
How many points are scored for a free throw?
What sport does this team play?
How many halves are in a soccer game?
approaching.explanation: "How many points did each player score?" is statistical because different players will have different scores — there is variability in the data.
choiceFeedback: A free throw's points are fixed—does this question ask about variation?
What sport is played doesn't vary—do different people answer this differently?
Halves in a game is a rule—does it change from one observation to another?
hints: Re-read each question and ask: would different people or games give different answers, or is there just one fixed answer?
A statistical question expects variability — many answers that differ. Sort each choice into 'one fixed answer' or 'answers that vary'.
Test one: 'How many halves are in a soccer game?' Every game has the same number — no variability there. Check the other three the same way.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál de las siguientes es una pregunta estadística?
approaching.explanationEs: «¿Cuántos puntos anotó cada jugador?» es estadística porque distintos jugadores tendrán puntajes distintos: hay variabilidad en los datos.

approaching.stem: Which question is NOT a statistical question?
choices: How many innings are in a baseball game?
How many home runs did each player hit this year?
How many miles does each runner train per week?
How tall is each player on the basketball team?
approaching.explanation: "How many innings are in a baseball game?" has one fixed answer (9) — no variability. The other questions all produce different answers for different people.
choiceFeedback: Each player hit a different number of home runs—would the answer vary?
Different runners train different miles—would the data vary?
Each player has a different height—would the answers vary?
hints: Careful — this asks for the question that is NOT statistical: the one with a single fixed answer instead of varying data.
For each choice ask: 'Would each player or runner give a different number?' The odd one out is a rule of the game, not data you collect.
Start with 'How tall is each player?' — heights differ player to player, so that one IS statistical. Keep testing until one has just one answer.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál pregunta NO es una pregunta estadística?
approaching.explanationEs: «¿Cuántas entradas tiene un partido de béisbol?» tiene una sola respuesta fija (9): no hay variabilidad. Las otras preguntas dan respuestas distintas para distintas personas.
choicesEs: ¿Cuántas entradas tiene un partido de béisbol?
¿Cuántos jonrones bateó cada jugador este año?
¿Cuántas millas entrena cada corredor por semana?
¿Cuánto mide cada jugador del equipo de baloncesto?
hintsEs: Cuidado: se pide la pregunta que NO es estadística, la que tiene una sola respuesta fija en lugar de datos que varían.
En cada opción pregunta: '¿daría cada jugador o corredor un número distinto?' La que sobra es una regla del juego, no datos que recolectas.
Empieza con '¿Cuánto mide cada jugador?': las estaturas cambian de jugador a jugador, así que esa SÍ es estadística. Sigue probando hasta hallar una con una sola respuesta.

approaching.stem: Why is 'How many hours of sleep did each student get last night?' a statistical question?
choices: Because different students got different amounts of sleep
Because it asks about sleep
Because hours are numbers
Because the answer is always 8 hours
approaching.explanation: A statistical question anticipates variability — different students slept different amounts, so the data will vary.
choiceFeedback: Sleep is a topic, not why it's statistical—which choice describes variability?
Hours are numbers, but are they used only in statistical questions?
If everyone slept 8 hours, would this be a statistical question?
hints: The question asks WHY it's statistical — focus on what happens when many students answer, not on the topic of sleep.
Think: if you asked every student how long they slept, would you get one number or many different numbers? That idea is called variability.
Picture asking 5 classmates their sleep hours and listing the numbers. Notice whether the list is all the same or varied — that's the key idea.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Por qué «¿Cuántas horas durmió cada estudiante anoche?» es una pregunta estadística?
approaching.explanationEs: Una pregunta estadística anticipa variabilidad: distintos estudiantes durmieron cantidades distintas, así que los datos van a variar.
choicesEs: Porque distintos estudiantes durmieron cantidades distintas
Porque pregunta sobre el sueño
Porque las horas son números
Porque la respuesta siempre es 8 horas
hintsEs: La pregunta es POR QUÉ es estadística: concéntrate en lo que pasa cuando muchos estudiantes responden, no en el tema del sueño.
Piensa: si le preguntaras a cada estudiante cuánto durmió, ¿obtendrías un número o muchos números distintos? Esa idea se llama variabilidad.
Imagina preguntar a 5 compañeros sus horas de sueño y anotar los números. Fíjate si la lista es toda igual o variada: esa es la idea clave.

approaching.stem: Match each question to its type.

pairs.left: How tall is each swimmer on the team?
What color is the team mascot?
pairs.leftEs: ¿De qué color es la mascota del equipo?

pairs.left: How many laps does each runner complete?
How many players are on a soccer team?
pairs.leftEs: ¿Cuántos jugadores hay en un equipo de fútbol?

approaching.hint: Look for words like "each" or measurements of individuals—those signal variability.
hints: Read each question on the left and underline the word 'each' when you see it — it's a clue that many people are being measured.
Sort by asking: does this question collect data from many individuals (varies), or state one fact with a single answer (doesn't vary)?
Start with 'What color is the team mascot?' — one mascot, one color, so match it to Not Statistical. Do the rest one question at a time.
approaching.stemEs: Empareja cada pregunta con su tipo.
approaching.explanation: A question is statistical when the answers are expected to differ from person to person, and non-statistical when there is one fixed answer for everyone.
approaching.explanationEs: Una pregunta es estadística cuando se espera que las respuestas sean distintas de una persona a otra, y no estadística cuando hay una sola respuesta fija para todos.

approaching.instructions: Sort these questions into Statistical or Not Statistical.

categories.label: Statistical Question
items: How many books did each student read this month?
What grade did each student earn on the test?
itemsEs: ¿Cuántos libros leyó cada estudiante este mes?
¿Qué calificación obtuvo cada estudiante en el examen?

categories.label: Not a Statistical Question
items: How many days are in a week?
itemsEs: ¿Cuál es la mascota de la escuela?

hints: Statistical questions expect different answers from different people or observations.
Non-statistical questions have one fixed answer that doesn't change.
approaching.label: Sort each question by type.
approaching.explanation: The books-read and test-grade questions ask about each student, so different students give different answers — that variability is what makes a question statistical. The number of days in a week and the school mascot each have one fixed answer that never changes, so they are not statistical.
approaching.explanationEs: Las preguntas sobre los libros leídos y la calificación del examen preguntan por cada estudiante, así que distintos estudiantes dan respuestas distintas; esa variabilidad es lo que hace que una pregunta sea estadística. El número de días de la semana y la mascota de la escuela tienen una sola respuesta fija que nunca cambia, así que no son estadísticas.
hintsEs: Las preguntas estadísticas esperan respuestas distintas de personas u observaciones distintas.
Las preguntas no estadísticas tienen una sola respuesta fija que no cambia.

approaching.title: Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Question
workedExample.work: How tall is each player on the basketball team?
workedExample.workEs: ¿Cuánto mide cada jugador del equipo de básquetbol?

workedExample.label: Student decision
workedExample.work: This is NOT a statistical question.
workedExample.workEs: Esta NO es una pregunta estadística.

workedExample.label: Student reason
workedExample.work: Height is just one number, so every answer will be the same.
workedExample.workEs: La estatura es un solo número, así que todas las respuestas serán iguales.

approaching.correctWork: The reason is wrong. The question asks about EACH player, and different players have different heights — for example 58 in, 60 in, 63 in, 65 in. Because the answers vary from player to player, this IS a statistical question.
hints: The word "each" is a clue that you need data from many players.
Ask yourself: will every player give the same height, or different heights?
approaching.explanation: The reasoning step claims every answer will be the same, but the question asks about EACH player and players have different heights — 58 in, 60 in, 63 in, 65 in. Because the answers vary from player to player, the question is statistical after all.
approaching.explanationEs: El paso del razonamiento dice que todas las respuestas serán iguales, pero la pregunta es por CADA jugador y los jugadores tienen estaturas distintas: 58 in, 60 in, 63 in, 65 in. Como las respuestas varían de un jugador a otro, la pregunta sí es estadística.
approaching.correctWorkEs: La razón está mal. La pregunta es sobre CADA jugador, y jugadores distintos tienen estaturas distintas — por ejemplo 58 pulg, 60 pulg, 63 pulg, 65 pulg. Como las respuestas varían de jugador a jugador, esta SÍ es una pregunta estadística.

onLevel.stem: A coach asks: "How many hours does each athlete on the track team sleep the night before a meet?" Why is this a statistical question?
choices: Because the answers will vary from athlete to athlete
Because it is about sports
Because it has a numerical answer
Because the coach asked it
onLevel.explanation: A statistical question anticipates variability. Different athletes sleep different amounts, so the data collected will vary.
choiceFeedback: Sports is a topic—what specific part makes this statistical?
Numbers can appear in fixed-answer questions too—why is this different?
Who asks the question doesn't determine if it's statistical—look deeper.
hints: Notice the words 'each athlete' — the coach plans to collect one number from every runner on the team.
Ask: will all athletes report the same hours of sleep? What we call it when collected answers differ is the key to this question.
Imagine the coach's list: 8, 6.5, 9, 7 hours from different athletes. The first step is naming what a changing list like that shows.
onLevel.stemEs: Un entrenador pregunta: «¿Cuántas horas duerme cada atleta del equipo de atletismo la noche antes de una competencia?» ¿Por qué es una pregunta estadística?
onLevel.explanationEs: Una pregunta estadística anticipa variabilidad. Distintos atletas duermen cantidades distintas, así que los datos recolectados van a variar.
choicesEs: Porque las respuestas variarán de un atleta a otro
Porque es sobre deportes
Porque tiene una respuesta numérica
Porque la hizo el entrenador
hintsEs: Fíjate en las palabras 'cada atleta': el entrenador planea recolectar un número de cada corredor del equipo.
Pregunta: ¿todos los atletas reportarán las mismas horas de sueño? Cómo se llama cuando las respuestas recolectadas difieren es la clave de esta pregunta.
Imagina la lista del entrenador: 8, 6.5, 9, 7 horas de distintos atletas. El primer paso es nombrar lo que muestra una lista que cambia así.

rows.question: How many push-ups can each student do in one minute?
rows.why: Different students can do different amounts — there is variability.

rows.question: How many sides does a basketball court have?
rows.why: There is one fixed answer (4 sides) — no variability.

rows.question: How far does each player kick the ball?
rows.why: Different players kick different distances — the data varies.

onLevel.label: Decide if each question is statistical and explain why.
hints: For each row, check whether the question asks about many people ('each student', 'each player') or one fixed fact about the game.
Column 2: write Yes if answers would differ person to person, No if there's only one possible answer. Column 3: explain using 'varies' or 'fixed'.
Row 1: push-ups in one minute — could two students do different amounts? Write Yes or No, then explain why in the last column.
onLevel.explanation: Rows 1 and 3 ask about each student and each player, so the push-up counts and kick distances differ from person to person — that variability makes both statistical. Row 2 asks how many sides a basketball court has, which is always 4, so there is nothing to vary and the answer is No.
onLevel.explanationEs: Las filas 1 y 3 preguntan por cada estudiante y por cada jugador, así que la cantidad de lagartijas y las distancias de las patadas cambian de una persona a otra; esa variabilidad hace que las dos sean estadísticas. La fila 2 pregunta cuántos lados tiene una cancha de básquetbol, que siempre son 4, así que no hay nada que varíe y la respuesta es No.
onLevel.labelEs: Decide si cada pregunta es estadística y explica por qué.
hintsEs: En cada fila, revisa si la pregunta trata de muchas personas ('cada estudiante', 'cada jugador') o de un dato fijo del juego.
Columna 2: escribe Sí si las respuestas difieren de persona a persona, y No si solo hay una respuesta posible. Columna 3: explica usando 'varía' o 'fija'.
Fila 1: lagartijas en un minuto — ¿podrían dos estudiantes hacer cantidades distintas? Escribe Sí o No y luego explica por qué en la última columna.

onLevel.stem: Match each question with what makes it statistical or not.

pairs.left: How fast does each sprinter run the 100m?
pairs.leftEs: ¿Qué tan rápido corre cada velocista los 100m?

pairs.left: How long is an Olympic pool?
How many goals did each player score this season?
pairs.leftEs: ¿Cuántos goles anotó cada jugador esta temporada?

pairs.left: How many innings are in a baseball game?
pairs.leftEs: ¿Cuántas entradas tiene un juego de béisbol?

onLevel.hint: Read each description—does it ask about many cases with different answers?
hints: Each right-side card already tells you the reason: 'Variability' or 'One answer.' Your job is deciding which reason fits each question.
Test each left question: does it measure many sprinters or players (answers differ), or state one fact like a pool's length (one answer)?
Start with 'How long is an Olympic pool?' — every Olympic pool is the same length, so pair it with a 'One answer' card. Continue down the list.
onLevel.stemEs: Empareja cada pregunta con lo que la hace estadística o no.
onLevel.explanation: The deciding feature is variability: if asking many people would produce different answers, the question is statistical; if everyone gives the same answer, it is not.
onLevel.explanationEs: La característica que decide es la variabilidad: si preguntarle a muchas personas daría respuestas distintas, la pregunta es estadística; si todos dan la misma respuesta, no lo es.

onLevel.instructions: Each non-statistical question below has been rewritten to become statistical. Match the original to its rewritten version.

categories.label: Original: 'How many students are in 6th grade?'
items: Rewritten: 'How many hours does each 6th grader study per week?'
itemsEs: Reescrita: '¿Cuántas horas estudia cada estudiante de 6.º por semana?'

categories.label: Original: 'What time does school start?'
items: Rewritten: 'What time does each student arrive at school?'
categories.labelEs: Original: '¿A qué hora empieza la escuela?'
itemsEs: Reescrita: '¿A qué hora llega cada estudiante a la escuela?'

hints: To make a question statistical, add variability by asking about 'each' person or observation.
The rewritten version should produce different answers for different people.
onLevel.label: Match each non-statistical question with its statistical rewrite.
onLevel.explanation: Each rewrite keeps the same topic but shifts the question to 'each' person, which is what creates variability. Counting 6th graders gives one number, but the hours each 6th grader studies differ; the school's start time is fixed, but the time each student arrives differs.
onLevel.explanationEs: Cada versión reescrita mantiene el mismo tema, pero cambia la pregunta a 'cada' persona, que es lo que crea variabilidad. Contar a los estudiantes de sexto grado da un solo número, pero las horas que estudia cada estudiante de sexto son distintas; la hora de entrada de la escuela es fija, pero la hora en que llega cada estudiante es distinta.
onLevel.labelEs: Une cada pregunta no estadística con su versión reescrita como estadística.
hintsEs: Para hacer estadística una pregunta, agrega variabilidad preguntando por 'cada' persona u observación.
La versión reescrita debe producir respuestas distintas para personas distintas.

onLevel.title: Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Question
workedExample.work: How many points does the team need to win a game?
workedExample.workEs: ¿Cuántos puntos necesita el equipo para ganar un partido?

workedExample.label: Student decision
workedExample.workEs: Esta SÍ es una pregunta estadística.

workedExample.label: Student reason
workedExample.work: It is about basketball and the answer is a number, so it must be statistical.
workedExample.workEs: Es sobre básquetbol y la respuesta es un número, así que debe ser estadística.

onLevel.correctWork: The reason is wrong. Being about basketball or having a number does not make a question statistical. "How many points does the team need to win a game?" has one fixed answer — you only need to score more than the other team — so the answers do not vary. This is NOT a statistical question.
hints: Numbers and a sports topic do not automatically make a question statistical.
Ask whether the answers would VARY. If there is one fixed answer, it is not statistical.
onLevel.explanation: The reasoning step says a basketball topic and a numerical answer make a question statistical, but neither one does. The points needed to win has a single fixed answer — more than the other team — so nothing varies, and the question is not statistical.
onLevel.explanationEs: El paso del razonamiento dice que hablar de básquetbol y tener una respuesta numérica hacen que una pregunta sea estadística, pero ninguna de las dos cosas lo hace. Los puntos que se necesitan para ganar tienen una sola respuesta fija —más que el otro equipo—, así que nada varía y la pregunta no es estadística.
onLevel.correctWorkEs: La razón está mal. Que sea sobre básquetbol o que la respuesta sea un número no hace estadística una pregunta. '¿Cuántos puntos necesita el equipo para ganar?' tiene una sola respuesta fija — solo necesitas anotar más que el otro equipo — así que las respuestas no varían. Esta NO es una pregunta estadística.

onLevel.stem: Which of these is a statistical question?
choices: What time is it right now?
How tall are the students in my class?
What is my shoe size?
What is 7 × 8?
onLevel.explanation: A statistical question anticipates variability — students' heights differ, so the data will vary.
choiceFeedback: What time it is right now doesn't vary—would collecting data help here?
Your shoe size is one fixed measurement—does it vary for different people?
Multiplication has one answer—would this question ever need data?
hints: Three of these have exactly one answer you could look up or compute. Find the one where collecting data from many people makes sense.
For each choice ask: 'If I surveyed my whole class, would I get a list of different numbers?' A statistical question needs that variety.
Test 'What is 7 × 8?' first — it has one answer no matter who you ask, so it can't be statistical. Apply the same test to the rest.
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Cuál de estas es una pregunta estadística?
onLevel.explanationEs: Una pregunta estadística anticipa variabilidad: las estaturas de los estudiantes son distintas, así que los datos van a variar.

onLevel.stem: Which of these would collect data that VARIES (making it a statistical question)?
choices: How many days are in one week?
How many siblings does each student in the class have?
How many minutes are in one hour?
What is 12 + 12?
onLevel.explanation: Number of siblings varies from student to student, so the collected data will vary — that makes it statistical. The others each have one fixed answer.
choiceFeedback: Days in a week is constant—does it vary?
Minutes in an hour don't change—does it vary?
12+12 always equals 24—would data vary?
hints: The capital word VARIES is the clue — you need the question whose answers change from student to student.
Check each choice: is it a fact of the calendar, clock, or math (never changes), or a survey where classmates would answer differently?
Start with 'How many days are in one week?' — that never changes, so its data can't vary. Keep testing each choice the same way.
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Cuál de estas recolectaría datos que VARÍAN (lo que la convierte en una pregunta estadística)?
onLevel.explanationEs: El número de hermanos varía de un estudiante a otro, así que los datos recolectados van a variar, y eso la hace estadística. Las demás tienen una sola respuesta fija.
choicesEs: ¿Cuántos días tiene una semana?
¿Cuántos hermanos tiene cada estudiante del salón?
¿Cuántos minutos tiene una hora?
¿Cuánto es 12 + 12?
hintsEs: La palabra en mayúsculas VARÍA es la pista: necesitas la pregunta cuyas respuestas cambian de estudiante a estudiante.
Revisa cada opción: ¿es un dato del calendario, del reloj o de matemáticas (nunca cambia), o una encuesta donde los compañeros responderían distinto?
Empieza con '¿Cuántos días tiene una semana?': eso nunca cambia, así que sus datos no pueden variar. Sigue probando cada opción igual.

extending.title: Find the Reasoning Error

workedExample.label: Question
workedExample.work: How many touchdowns did the quarterback throw this season?
workedExample.workEs: ¿Cuántos touchdowns lanzó el mariscal de campo esta temporada?

workedExample.label: Student says
workedExample.work: This is NOT a statistical question.
workedExample.workEs: Esta NO es una pregunta estadística.

workedExample.label: Reason
workedExample.work: It only asks about one player, so there is no variability.
workedExample.workEs: Solo pregunta por un jugador, así que no hay variabilidad.

extending.correctWork: Even though it asks about one player, "this season" means multiple games. The number of touchdowns per game varies, so there IS variability in the data. This IS a statistical question.
hints: Think about whether the data collected would have different values across games.
The question asks about performance over a whole season — each game can have a different result.
extending.explanation: The reasoning step assumes one player means no variability, but 'this season' covers many games and the touchdown count changes from game to game. That game-to-game variation is real data variability, so the question is statistical.
extending.explanationEs: El paso del razonamiento supone que un solo jugador significa que no hay variabilidad, pero 'esta temporada' abarca muchos partidos y la cantidad de anotaciones cambia de un partido a otro. Esa variación de partido a partido es variabilidad real en los datos, así que la pregunta sí es estadística.
extending.correctWorkEs: Aunque pregunta por un solo jugador, 'esta temporada' significa varios partidos. El número de touchdowns por partido varía, así que SÍ hay variabilidad en los datos. Esta SÍ es una pregunta estadística.

extending.prompt: Write one statistical question and one non-statistical question about your school's cafeteria. Explain why each question is or is not statistical, and describe what the data would look like for the statistical question.
extending.sentenceFrame: Statistical question: ___. This is statistical because ___. The data might look like: ___. Non-statistical question: ___. This is not statistical because ___.
extending.hint: Start by thinking of a question where answers would be different for different people.
hints: You need TWO questions about the cafeteria: one where classmates would answer differently, and one with a single fixed answer.
Brainstorm cafeteria data: minutes in line, lunches bought per week. For the non-statistical one, use a fixed fact like the number of tables.
Start your first sentence: 'How many ___ does each student ___?' Using 'each student' builds in variability — then describe the different answers.
extending.explanation: A strong statistical cafeteria question asks about each person, such as 'How many minutes does each student wait in the lunch line?' — the data would be a spread of values like 2, 5, 7, and 11 minutes. A non-statistical one, such as 'How many tables are in the cafeteria?', has a single fixed answer, so there is nothing to collect or compare.
extending.explanationEs: Una buena pregunta estadística sobre la cafetería pregunta por cada persona, como '¿Cuántos minutos espera cada estudiante en la fila del almuerzo?': los datos serían valores variados como 2, 5, 7 y 11 minutos. Una no estadística, como '¿Cuántas mesas hay en la cafetería?', tiene una sola respuesta fija, así que no hay nada que recolectar ni comparar.
extending.promptEs: Escribe una pregunta estadística y una pregunta no estadística sobre la cafetería de tu escuela. Explica por qué cada pregunta es o no es estadística y describe cómo se verían los datos de la pregunta estadística.
hintsEs: Necesitas DOS preguntas sobre la cafetería: una donde los compañeros responderían distinto y otra con una sola respuesta fija.
Piensa en datos de cafetería: minutos en la fila, almuerzos comprados por semana. Para la no estadística, usa un dato fijo como el número de mesas.
Empieza tu primera oración: '¿Cuántos ___ hace cada estudiante ___?' Usar 'cada estudiante' incorpora variabilidad; luego describe las respuestas distintas.

rows.nonStatistical: How many players are on the team?
rows.rewritten: How many minutes does each player on the team play per game?
rows.variability: Different players get different amounts of playing time.

rows.nonStatistical: What sport does this league play?
rows.rewritten: How many games does each team in this league win per season?
rows.variability: Different teams win different numbers of games.

extending.label: Rewrite each non-statistical question to make it statistical and explain the variability.
hints: Each row starts with a one-answer question. Your rewrite should ask about MANY players or teams so the answers can differ.
A reliable trick: add the word 'each' plus a measurement — 'How many ___ does each ___...?' Then describe who would give different answers.
Row 1: 'How many players are on the team?' has one count. First step — ask something measurable about each player, like points scored per game.
extending.explanation: Each rewrite trades a one-answer count for a measurement taken on every member of the group. 'How many players are on the team?' becomes minutes played per game, which varies because starters play more than bench players, and the league's sport becomes wins per team, which varies because some teams win more games than others.
extending.explanationEs: Cada versión reescrita cambia un conteo de una sola respuesta por una medición tomada a cada integrante del grupo. '¿Cuántos jugadores hay en el equipo?' se convierte en los minutos jugados por partido, que varían porque los titulares juegan más que los suplentes, y el deporte de la liga se convierte en los partidos ganados por equipo, que varían porque algunos equipos ganan más que otros.
extending.labelEs: Reescribe cada pregunta no estadística para volverla estadística y explica la variabilidad.
hintsEs: Cada fila empieza con una pregunta de una sola respuesta. Tu versión nueva debe preguntar por MUCHOS jugadores o equipos para que las respuestas difieran.
Un truco confiable: agrega la palabra 'cada' más una medida — '¿Cuántos ___ hace cada ___?' Luego describe quién daría respuestas distintas.
Fila 1: '¿Cuántos jugadores hay en el equipo?' tiene un solo conteo. Primer paso: pregunta algo medible de cada jugador, como puntos anotados por partido.

extending.stem: A survey asks 30 students how many books they read last month, collecting 30 answers. What makes this a statistical question?
choices: It is about books
Everyone reads the same number
The answers vary from student to student
It has exactly one correct answer
extending.explanation: Statistical questions anticipate variability in the data collected across many people.
choiceFeedback: A topic doesn't determine if a question is statistical—what else matters?
If everyone read the same number, would this be statistical?
One answer means fixed, not statistical—but do the answers vary here?
hints: Re-read the setup: 30 students each report how many books they read — that's 30 separate answers collected.
Ask what those 30 answers probably look like: all identical, or a mix like 2, 5, 0, 7...? That property is what makes a question statistical.
First step: picture the list of 30 numbers. Decide whether the list is fixed or full of different values, then match that idea to a choice.
extending.stemEs: Una encuesta pregunta a 30 estudiantes cuántos libros leyeron el mes pasado y recoge 30 respuestas. ¿Qué hace que esta sea una pregunta estadística?
extending.explanationEs: Las preguntas estadísticas anticipan variabilidad en los datos recolectados entre muchas personas.
choicesEs: Es sobre libros
Todos leen la misma cantidad
Las respuestas varían de un estudiante a otro
Tiene exactamente una respuesta correcta
hintsEs: Vuelve a leer el planteamiento: 30 estudiantes reportan cada uno cuántos libros leyeron; eso son 30 respuestas separadas recolectadas.
Pregunta cómo se verían probablemente esas 30 respuestas: ¿todas idénticas o una mezcla como 2, 5, 0, 7…? Esa propiedad es lo que hace estadística a una pregunta.
Primer paso: imagina la lista de 30 números. Decide si la lista es fija o está llena de valores distintos, y luego une esa idea con una opción.

extending.stem: Which rewrite turns 'What is my resting heart rate?' into a statistical question?
choices: Is my heart rate high?
What is a heart rate?
What is the teacher's heart rate?
What are the resting heart rates of students in my class?
extending.explanation: Asking across many people, whose rates vary, makes the question statistical.
choiceFeedback: This still asks about one person—does one person's answer vary?
This still asks about one person—will the answer vary?
One person's rate doesn't vary—will you get different answers?
hints: The original question asks about ONE person's resting heart rate — one measurement, so no variability.
A statistical rewrite must gather data from many people whose numbers differ. Check each choice: how many people does it measure?
Test the first rewrite, 'Is my heart rate high?' — still one person, still one answer. Keep checking until a choice surveys a whole group.
extending.stemEs: ¿Cuál reescritura convierte «¿Cuál es mi frecuencia cardíaca en reposo?» en una pregunta estadística?
extending.explanationEs: Preguntar a muchas personas, cuyas frecuencias varían, es lo que hace que la pregunta sea estadística.

optionalActivity.name: Statistical or Not? Sports Sort
optionalActivity.intro: Step into the team's data room and decide which scouting questions are worth collecting data for.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Statistical Questions and Data is judging a question by its topic or its numbers instead of its variability. Students see a question about ONE player, ONE game, or ONE fixed fact — like "How many points does the team need to win a game?" — and call it statistical just because it has a number or is about sports. Or they see a question about a single player's whole season, like "How many touchdowns did the quarterback throw this season?", and call it NOT statistical because only one player is named, forgetting that a season covers many games with a different result each time. Both errors skip the real test: will the answers actually differ from case to case (game to game, player to player)? If yes, it is a statistical question; if there is one fixed answer, it is not.

diagram.title: Goals Scored This Season — One Dot per Player
diagram.caption: Every player answers the editor's question differently — the dots spread from 0 to 6 goals. The reporter's question has only one answer: the total.

connect.scenario: The school newspaper wants to write a story about the girls' soccer team. A reporter suggests asking: "How many goals has the team scored total?" The editor says they should ask: "How many goals did each player score this season?"
connect.promptQuestion: Which question is statistical? Why would the editor's question give the newspaper more interesting data?
connect.prompt: The reporter's question is ___ because ___. The editor's question is ___ because ___. The editor's question is better for a story because ___.

choices: 'How many goals did each player score this season?'
'How many goals has the team scored total?'
Both are statistical
Neither is statistical
check.explanation: A statistical question anticipates VARIABILITY — different answers from different players. Asking each player's goals produces many different numbers. The team total has exactly one answer.

check.stem: Why is the team total NOT a statistical question?
choices: Because it has exactly one answer, with no variability
Because totals are never useful
Because it is about soccer
Because you cannot count goals
check.explanation: Statistical questions expect a spread of answers. 'What is the total?' has a single fixed answer, so there is no distribution to describe.

check.stem: Which of these is a statistical question?
choices: How tall are the students in my class?
How tall am I?
What is today's date?
How many minutes are in an hour?
check.explanation: Different students have different heights, so that question produces a data set with variability. Each of the others has one fixed answer.

connect.modelAnswer: The reporter's question is NOT statistical — 'how many goals total' has exactly one answer. The editor's question IS statistical, because different players scored different numbers, so it produces a data set with variability. That spread is what makes a story: you can write about the top scorer, the typical player, and how evenly the scoring was shared.

exitTicket.stem:
Which question is a statistical question?
A) How many students are in the school?
B) How many hours does each student in 6th grade exercise per week?
C) What time does school start?
D) How many days are in a week?
choices: B) How many hours does each student exercise per week?
A) How many students are in the school?
C) What time does school start?
D) How many days are in a week?
exitTicket.explanation: "How many hours does each student exercise per week?" is statistical because different students exercise different amounts — the data has variability.
choiceFeedback: That has one exact answer — statistical questions expect varied data.
One fixed time isn't statistical — look for varying answers.
That's always 7 — statistical questions have answers that vary.
hints: Look for the question where you'd collect a different number from each 6th grader instead of looking up one fixed fact.
Sort the four options into 'one fixed answer' vs 'answers that vary.' Only one belongs in the 'varies' group — that's the statistical one.
First step: try option D — days in a week never changes, so it has no variability. Apply that same check to A, B, and C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a statistical question?
choices: How many points are scored for a free throw?
How many points did each player score this season?
What sport does this team play?
How many halves are in a soccer game?
questions.explanation: "How many points did each player score?" is statistical because different players will have different scores — there is variability in the data.

questions.stem: Why is 'How many hours of sleep did each student get last night?' a statistical question?
choices: Because it asks about sleep
Because different students got different amounts of sleep
Because hours are numbers
Because the answer is always 8 hours
questions.explanation: A statistical question anticipates variability — different students slept different amounts, so the data will vary.

questions.stem: Which question is NOT a statistical question?
choices: How many home runs did each player hit this year?
How many innings are in a baseball game?
How many miles does each runner train per week?
How tall is each player on the basketball team?
questions.explanation: "How many innings are in a baseball game?" has one fixed answer (9) — no variability. The other questions all produce different answers for different people.

mission.title: Scout the Hardwood
mission.story: You are the new data analyst for the Riverside Hoops youth league. The head coach drops a stack of questions on your desk — some will yield rich data full of variety, others just one fixed fact. Master statistical questions and you decide what the front office actually investigates.
mission.objective: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones so the team collects data worth analyzing.

scenes.name: Scouting Report

finale.title: Report Filed!
finale.text: Your scouting plan captured exactly the data the coaches needed, and the team is climbing the standings. Riverside Hoops just made you lead analyst — because you know which questions reveal real variability.
